turns.replyText:
Can you explain the main options in simple terms?

Love this question, and you’re not alone in feeling a bit lost at the start.

Here are the main choices in very simple terms:

Where the rose will grow
In the ground: Best long-term option. Roses get big, deep roots and are usually happiest here.
In a large container: Good if you’re renting, have a patio, or poor soil. Use a big pot (about 10 gallons) with good quality potting soil.
Rose “shape” or growth habit
Climbing roses: Long, flexible canes that need support (fence, arch, trellis). Great if you want a wall or arch of roses.
Shrub/bush roses: Rounded plants, good for most gardens and borders. This is usually the easiest place to start.
Groundcover/landscape roses: Low, spreading plants that cover an area. Good for slopes, edges, or low-maintenance spots.
Hybrid tea roses: Tall, upright plants with classic long-stemmed blooms (the “florist” look). Great if you want cut flowers for vases.
How often they bloom
Repeat/continuous bloomers: Flower through the season, either non-stop or in waves. Easiest and most rewarding for beginners.
Once-blooming roses: A big flush of blooms once a year, then mostly green the rest of the season. Beautiful, but less “always blooming.”
What you care about most
Low maintenance & forgiving: Choose easy, beginner-friendly varieties.
Big fragrance: Look for roses described as “strong fragrance.”
Cut flowers: Look for hybrid teas or roses noted as good for cutting.

To make this easier, we have a curated group of beginner-friendly roses here: Easy-to-Grow Roses.

turns.replyText:
Is there anything else a beginner needs to get started?

You’re asking all the right questions. Let’s keep this simple and beginner‑ and budget‑friendly.

I’ll break it into:

Must‑haves

Nice‑to‑have extras

Simple learning resources

Must‑haves These are the basics you really do need:

A good planting spot or pot

In the ground: A sunny spot (at least 6 hours of sun) with soil that drains well and doesn’t stay soggy.
In a pot: A large container (about 10 gallons) with drainage holes and good quality potting soil.

Basic tools

Small shovel or trowel for digging the hole.
Hand pruners for pruning (cutting back canes to shape the plant and encourage new growth) and deadheading (removing spent flowers so new ones form).

Mulch

A 2–3 inch layer of mulch (like bark fines or wood chips) around the base helps keep moisture in and roots cool, and reduces weeds.

Fertilizer (this is important)

Roses are heavy feeders, so they do need regular nutrients.
For the first year, a liquid fertilizer is easiest for beginners: you mix it with water and apply around the root zone.
You can use our fertilizers or any rose‑appropriate fertilizer you prefer; the key is to follow the label directions and not overdo it.
Nice‑to‑have extras (helpful but not required) These are optional, especially if you’re watching costs, but they can give your rose a boost:
Soil amendments (mixed into the planting hole or top few inches of soil):
Bone meal: Helps with strong root development.
Cow manure: Adds long‑lasting nutrients to the soil.
Mint compost: Improves soil structure and aeration; can also be used as a top dressing to protect roots.
Worm castings: Gentle, natural nutrients and better soil aeration.

You absolutely do not have to buy all of these to succeed. Many beginners do very well with:

A good planting spot or pot
Mulch
One simple liquid fertilizer

Then you can add amendments later as you feel more confident.

turns.replyText:
How do I use it properly the very first time?

Great question, and you’re smart to think about this before the rose arrives.

Since we’ve been talking about a beginner rose, I’ll walk you through how to handle your new rose on Day 1.

Unpack and hydrate
Take the rose out of the shipping box and compostable bag or plastic pot.
Water it well until water runs out the bottom of the container it arrived in.
Keep it outdoors in a bright spot (not baking hot mid‑day sun right away) while you get the planting spot or pot ready.
Decide where it’s going
Roses must live outdoors.
Full sun is best: at least 6 hours of direct sunlight a day.
Planting basics (same idea for ground or pot)
Loosen the roots gently with your fingers if they are tight.
Set the rose so the existing soil line on the plant is level with the surrounding soil.
Backfill with good soil (or potting soil for containers), pressing gently to remove big air pockets.
Water deeply again.
Add a 2–3 inch layer of mulch around (but not touching) the stems to keep moisture in.
First fertilizer use
For a brand‑new planting, keep it simple.
Wait until you see a bit of new growth (a few inches and a leaflet with 5–7 little leaves) before you start fertilizing regularly.
Use a liquid fertilizer mixed with water according to the label, and pour it around the base of the plant, not on the leaves.
First few weeks
Keep the soil evenly moist but not soggy. Check with your finger; if the top inch feels dry, it’s time to water.
Don’t worry if it doesn’t bloom right away; it will focus on roots first.
